description: We are a tech-driven CSE student team participating in the SphereX and PlanetX challenges. Our project focuses on breaking down complex NASA astronomical data and mission telemetry into a highly interactive, visual platform. By simplifying intricate cosmic concepts and space exploration data, we aim to make it easily understandable, engaging, and educational for children, sparking their curiosity and building a strong, lasting interest in space science.
summary:
Cosmic Hunt is a free, browser-based 3D space exploration game designed to make real infrared astronomy accessible and fun for students, teachers, and curious beginners worldwide.
Inspired by NASA’s SPHEREx mission, complex infrared spectroscopy is often difficult for young learners to visualize. To bridge this gap, Cosmic Hunt turns scientific data analysis into an interactive mission. Players use a SPHEREx-style infrared scanner and spectrum graph to compare wavelength peaks (such as a 3.3 µm signature) and track down a hidden "Planet X" without needing any special equipment or prior knowledge.
Beyond the core hunt, the platform features a 3D solar system, Exoplanet Atlas, deep-space views, and an "Ask AI" guide powered by live NASA datasets (GIBS, Trek, APOD, and NASA Image Library). With intuitive, mobile-friendly controls and voice support, Cosmic Hunt empowers educators anywhere to teach real space science in minutes.
details:
The challenge we answered-

NASA's SPHEREx telescope, launched in 2025, is mapping the whole sky in 102 infrared colors (0.75 to 5 micrometers). That is exciting science, but it is hard for students to picture. We wanted to turn it into something children can play: Cosmic Hunt, a mission where the player uses SPHEREx-style infrared vision to find a hidden "Planet X".

How it works-

The player starts with a mission briefing: mysterious objects, including Planet X, are hiding behind infrared light. A Data Clue Box gives the target signal, an infrared peak at 3.3 µm. The player turns on the SPHEREx panel's Infrared Vision, clicks objects in the sky, and compares each object's spectrum graph with the clue. When the signature matches, Planet X is "LOCKED", a reveal explains what we still don't know about it (distance, mass and size), and the player is told they discovered a world "just like a NASA scientist".

Around this game loop we built a full 3D space explorer, all running in the browser with Three.js and no install:

- Exoplanet Atlas: an orrery and planet viewer, with structure and detail views and size comparisons.

- Earth and Satellites: a live-data Earth globe with satellites.

- Milky Way and Galaxies: deep-space modes, including a Sagittarius A* black-hole view, nebulae and galaxies, each with its own scene and camera.

- Mission Control: today's NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, an "Ask NASA" tab with matching records, and a "Sounds" tab with NASA audio.

- Ask AI: a short, friendly answer box. It works with built-in answers by default, and uses Claude if a visitor pastes their own key (stored only in their browser).

NASA data we use-

NASA GIBS (Earth imagery, including a land-surface-temperature "infrared scanner" layer), NASA Trek (Mars and Moon mosaics), the NASA Image and Video Library, the APOD API, the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, and the SPHEREx mission page. Sound and visuals are generated in the browser (Web Audio, Canvas, WebGL), so the game stays lightweight.

Who it helps-

Students, teachers and curious beginners. The interface uses a multilingual- friendly font, spoken voice lines, sound effects and tap-friendly controls, so it works on a phone as well as a computer. Teachers can use it as a five-minute introduction to infrared astronomy and spectra.

What we'd build next-

- Replace the typed-in planet values with live data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

- Use real SPHEREx spectra as they are released, so each hunt is based on real measurements.

- Add a server proxy so NASA data works reliably everywhere.

- Add more hunts, difficulty levels and a progress or badge system.

- Add full Bengali and other language support, and classroom materials.

- Add a multiplayer or classroom leaderboard mode.

AI tools were used to assist with code debugging and text refinement, alongside an optional Claude-powered 'Ask AI' helper.
